newsitem.title: USA: Greek minister defends Turkey over EU move.
newsitem.headline: Greek minister defends Turkey over EU move.

text.p: Greek Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos on Thursday issued an unusual defence of Turkey, his country's traditional adversary, as a state that belongs to Europe and deserves inclusion in the European Union.

"Turkey certainly belongs to Europe. It's a big part of European history and Greece shall never change its mind about that because if Turkey is not a part of European history then Greece is not a part of European history," he told reporters after talks with U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.

Pangalos was responding to a question about a statement issued on Tuesday in Brussels by leading centrist EU politicians who gave Turkey its bluntest warning to date that it would be locked out of the EU.
Senior politicians said there was consensus at a meeting of the mainly Christian Democrat European People's Party (EPP) that Turkey was not qualified to join.
A spokesman for the Greek Embassy in Washington said Pangalos was not asked about Turkish membership of the EU, and his remark was about Turkey generally.
Asked if Pangalos was advocating Turkish EU membership, spokesman Theodosis Demetracopoulos said: "He did not say that."

"We have not said that Turkey should never become a member. We have said that certain conditions have to be met before that" such as resolution of disputes over Cyprus, the Aegean and territorial claims, the spokesman said.
If those conditions were met "it would be a completely different ball-game," he told Reuters.
The United States strongly supports Turkey's entrance into the EU and other western institutions. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns repeated that position on Thursday.

Turkish journalists said Pangalos' latest comment on Turkey was more conciliatory than previous remarks. But Burns said that in talks earlier with Albright, Pangalos "did not soften his position" and continued to strongly defend Greek nationalist interests.

Albright was reported by Burns to have urged Pangalos urgently to find a way to open a dialogue with Turkey on their many disputes, including those over the Aegean and Cyprus, which have caused fears of a war between the two NATO allies.
At a brief news conference before their talks, Albright reiterated keen U.S. interest in trying to resolve this year Greek-Turkish tensions over Cyprus and other issues.

Burns said she did not lay out a blueprint for action on any of the issues but stressed that "she felt it was incumbent on Greece and Turkey to get together and reduce the sense of tension (and) that this was an imperative that they get together to reduce some of the conflicts between them."
The United States has made specific proposal and now "we're looking for some ideas from them," Burns added.
